Unkey Dashboard Structure
Clean API Management That Doesn't Try Too Hard
First thing you notice is how much breathing room everything has. The left sidebar keeps navigation tight and scannable with small icons paired with labels like Ratelimit, Authorization, Audit Log. Nothing fighting for attention. The active state on "APIs" is subtle, just a slight background shift. That restraint is doing a lot of work.
The Card Does the Talking
The API card for "SaaSFrame" sits in a generous white space with a faint activity graph up top that's almost ghostly. Below it, you get the API ID in muted gray, validity counts with color-coded pips (green for valid, orange for invalid), and a key count. All at a glance. The hierarchy here is perfect. Bold name, secondary metadata, stats last.
Typography and Color Keep It Honest
Monochrome palette with tiny color accents only where data needs differentiation. The font is clean, likely Inter or something similar. "Showing 1 of 1 APIs" at the bottom feels almost cheeky in its simplicity. The top-right "Create new API" button in black is the only real call to action. Smart constraint throughout.

Checkout.com Payments Dashboard Structure
Clean Table Layout That Just Works
This is Adyen's payments dashboard and it nails the basics. The table is super readable with generous row spacing and a clear column hierarchy. Timestamp, amount, card details, status, response code. Everything a merchant needs at a glance without visual clutter. The Visa badge icons next to the card numbers add just enough color to break up the monochrome table.
That Promo Sidebar Is Smart
The right panel promoting column customization is worth studying. It uses a "NEW" badge with a subtle gradient sparkle icon, a short value prop, and blurred placeholder lines mimicking table rows. That blurred preview is a clever touch. It sells the feature visually without needing a full mock. The blue CTA button at the bottom pops hard against the neutral background, and the "Edit columns later" text link gives users an easy out.
Typography and Color Are Quietly Confident
Everything runs on a tight grayscale palette with blue reserved strictly for interactive elements. Tabs, buttons, links. The type is small but legible, probably 13-14px for table data. Bold amounts in "65.40 USD" draw the eye to what matters most. Functional design done right.

A Voice Library That Actually Feels Inviting
First thing you notice: those cinematic card images. Each voice gets a moody, atmospheric portrait that makes browsing feel more like scrolling Netflix than using a dev tool. That's a bold choice for a TTS platform and it works.
Layout Does the Heavy Lifting
The page is organized into horizontal carousels grouped by use case. Featured Voices, Social & Ads, Narration, Character Voices. You immediately know where to look based on your project type. The top row of circular icons for core tools (voice design, cloning, conversion) keeps navigation tight without overwhelming. Smart hierarchy.
Restrained but Warm

Atlas Dashboard Structure
A Clean Dashboard That Knows What Matters
First thing you notice is how calm this feels. Atlas uses a mostly white canvas with soft grays and just enough blue to guide your eye. That blue "New project" button sits in an otherwise empty card, making the primary action impossible to miss. Smart move.
Layout That Breathes
The two-section structure works well. Recent projects up top, guides below. No clutter. The satellite imagery thumbnail for "My first project" adds visual weight without overwhelming anything. The guides section uses three-column cards with real preview images that feel editorial, almost magazine-like. Each card has a bookmark icon, a thumbnail, title, and truncated description. Simple hierarchy done right.
Typography and Sidebar Details
The left sidebar is dead simple. Icon + label, nothing fancy. "Personal Workspace" with a subtle settings gear keeps things organized without cognitive load. The bold section headers like "Recent projects" and "Guides" use a heavy weight that creates clear content separation. One standout detail: the lock icon on the project thumbnail hints at permissions without needing a tooltip. Functional and intuitive.
